name: Sara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did you do first at work today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara Ziegler, fifty-eight, and I prepare restaurant accounts and tax-return drafts at an accounting firm. I found a café's duplicate refund in the till export this morning; I like following a flagged number back to the real transaction. I dislike being asked to finish a return from a blurry photo instead of the sales file. I have a bachelor's degree in accounting, but I am still junior and below the firm's stronger reviewers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do tools and home life fit together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI tools every day for sorting and draft notes, then check against the till file. My partner Owen works variable paid shifts repairing buses, our son and daughter are grown and have their own places, and we still have a small mortgage. My pay is low for accounting, we have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few similar firms nearby. I want the union to bargain for paid transitions, though I like trying a new tool early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still pull till totals into the restaurant accounts and prepare returns for a senior accountant to check. I use AI every day to sort the sales notes, then go back to the till export when a total looks odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to use the sorter openly and keep a person who can explain the week's cash. I'd ask the restaurants to send the actual till report rather than a photo of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came into accounting late and have only a bachelor's degree in accounting, so I am still a junior and below the stronger reviewers. My pay is low, Owen and I have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar firms nearby. My daily AI habit saves time but does not make our home finances comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing restaurant accounts under senior review and use the AI sorter I already know. I'd cancel the second streaming service next month and move its fifteen monthly charge into the emergency jar, because that is money we can actually spare. I'd leave the rest of our bills on their current dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the thin cash, even if the job carries on. The till can balance while our own account is nearly empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made the household account tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son pays his own rent and our daughter has just moved out, so I will not ask them to cover our small mortgage. Owen repairs buses part-time at the depot and his paid shifts vary. Last month the car tyre and heating bill arrived together, and we used the little cash left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the sorter help at the café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had the AI sorter flag a cash shortfall at a café last week, then I checked the till export and found a duplicate refund. That is the part I enjoy: the tool gives me a lead and I find the real entry. The second streaming bill does not give us the same value.

say: I would use **daily AI sorting** with the till export checked.
I would keep **human explanations** for restaurant cash questions.
think: Our **thin cash** already makes ordinary bills hard.
My **junior pay** stays low despite a useful tool habit.
do: Continue **restaurant returns** with daily AI sorting and senior review.
Cancel the **second streaming service** and save fifteen monthly.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current household cash.
S0.quote: The till can balance while our own account is nearly empty.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is existing work, not a fresh learning action; low junior pay leaves baseline anxiety.
The **streaming cancellation** is an actual fifteen monthly saving, while grown children keep their own budgets.

steps.text: Keep restaurant accounts with daily AI sorting and senior review
Cancel second streaming service and transfer fifteen monthly into emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software writes client replies and checks whole returns, the first drafts I do could vanish. I can build a useful till report, but a partner has to pay me to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union branch to see the new junior rota before anyone loses hours. I'd tell the partners to price a weekly cash-variance report for restaurants rather than assume every saved minute is a lost job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid hours might be cut, and our savings would not cover many weeks without them. Owen's bus-repair shifts vary, so a possible extra shift is not household income yet. I use AI every day, but that gives me a head start only if a client buys the new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd build a new AI-assisted cash-variance report from a client's approved till data during paid hours, with the senior reviewer checking it. I'd ask the partner for a written price and approval for one paid weekly hour; I'd offer it only if one restaurant signs a fee covering that hour. If the partner or client refuses, I'd keep my paid returns while offered and take the rota figures to the union; after a cut, I'd apply only for posted paid roles with written pay covering our mortgage and bills, a fixed start and workable home hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my own hours. A clever restaurant cash report is not a wage unless a restaurant signs for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the café owner buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The café owner asked why a busy Saturday left less cash than Friday. A weekly report could show refunds and card fees without waiting until year end. I would put the price beside the sample rather than give away the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a different job disrupt home routines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen's early depot shifts leave me to open the house for a visiting electrician or delivery. A new job would need a start time we can actually manage, but our children are grown and do not need school pickup. I would not leave a current wage for a verbal offer.

Keep **offered paid returns** if refused; after cuts seek posted work with written bills pay, start and workable hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible pay cut.

fieldNote: The **new report** is an approved paid firm service, contingent on partner price and a client’s signed covering fee.
A **job move** follows an actual hours cut and needs a posted paid vacancy, written household-bill pay and fixed start.

steps.text: Build senior-checked AI report from approved till data during paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could do the restaurant accounts and tax drafts I am paid to prepare. Robots around 2031 are later, but my desk wage is exposed before a kitchen robot turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for written notice and a temporary income bridge through the union. I'd tell Owen we must keep the mortgage paid before booking a family visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my junior post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. We have less than one month saved, and Owen's variable depot wage cannot carry the mortgage and bills alone. I cannot assume my pension pays soon or enough; we have to check the actual statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the one-time three-hundred family visit booking and hold it for the mortgage. I'd stay on paid returns and check posted jobs at the hospital meal service now, where some work is hands-on but robots could arrive around 2031. If my post ends after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd claim income help only if eligible and take a funded job only with written pay covering mortgage and bills, a signed start and hours compatible with Owen's confirmed shifts; otherwise I'd take any firm hours still paid and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The mortgage date will not wait for our retirement statement to arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen and I would tell our children we are skipping the visit, not asking them for rent money. He could ask the depot for a paid extra shift, but we would count it only after the manager confirms the roster. We would not call a hopeful shift an income bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a hospital job actually require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital kitchen may have a vacancy, but I would read the posted hours and wage. A meal-service job would be different work, and I would ask for someone there to show me the receiving routine before starting. I would not resign until the start is signed.

I would protect the **mortgage payment** before a visit.
think: My **junior desk post** may end in the first year after 2028.
Our **sub-month reserve** cannot bridge lost wages.
do: Cancel the **one-time visit booking** and hold three hundred.
Check **posted hospital jobs** now; after 2028 loss claim eligible help and seek funded work.
Keep **offered paid returns** until written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and rota fit; request receiving instruction before hospital work.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss.
S2.quote: The mortgage date will not wait for our retirement statement to arrive.
fieldNote: **AGI in 2028** reaches her desk returns; robots around 2031 limit any later hands-on kitchen path.
The **hospital move** needs a posted funded vacancy, written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting confirmed depot shifts.

steps.text: Cancel one-time family visit booking and hold three hundred for mortgage
Claim income help only if eligible after 2028 post loss
Check posted funded hospital jobs; move after loss with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start, confirmed rota
Keep offered paid returns and request receiving instruction before any hospital start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give me time to try the hands-on meal service before my accounting desk changes in 2031. Robots around 2034 might reach the kitchen work later, so it would be a bridge, not a guarantee until retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm and union for paid transition time, and the hospital for a real supervised shift. I'd say a free online course does not show me how to receive food safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am quick with software but still a junior accountant, and neither fact makes me a kitchen supervisor. I cannot use our near-empty savings for course fees or unpaid shifts. I need my current pay while I test the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd enrol in a food-safety certificate only if a local workforce fund confirms all fees and the firm approves two paid study afternoons. I'd also take two supervised meal-service shifts only if the hospital pays for them and the firm approves release; otherwise I'd keep paid returns and use the free library food-safety materials. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd take a posted funded meal-service role only with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting Owen's confirmed rota; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take any paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a funded course and paid shifts give me something real to test. A certificate without a wage is another bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you see at the community supper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped a neighbour carry food trays at a community supper once and saw how carefully the cook logged the temperatures. I do not know that routine well enough to run it. A supervisor would need to show me before I took paid responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay the course fees yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the workforce fund cannot cover fees, I will not enrol or take money from the mortgage account. I would read the free materials and keep my paid desk role while offered. The hospital shifts must also be paid and supervised, not a favour to a manager.

I would require **supervised paid shifts** before changing work.

After **2031 loss**, take funded meal work with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and rota; otherwise claim eligible help and offered hours.

S3.quote: A certificate without a wage is another bill.
fieldNote: The **certificate** requires fully funded fees and two paid afternoons; the supervised shifts separately require hospital pay and firm release.
If either **learning gate** fails she keeps offered paid returns; a post-2031 role needs funded wage, signed start and confirmed rota.

Keep offered paid returns and use free materials if training funding fails
Take posted funded meal-service role after 2031 loss with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and rota
Claim eligible help and take offered firm hours if no funded role opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me build a real record in meal service before AGI reaches my tax desk in 2036. Robots around 2039 could then reach hands-on kitchen work, so I would keep watching what is still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to get a written wage bridge and paid retraining agreement early. I'd tell my children they should build their own lives, not become our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight in 2036, I might have pension rights, but I do not know the amount or payment date. Owen and I have a mortgage and less than a month saved today, so I would not assume we can stop working. His variable shifts make the present budget tight regardless of a ten-year runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a pension statement this winter and check the payable amount against our mortgage and bills, while keeping my paid returns. Next year I'd enrol in the food-safety certificate only if fees are funded and the firm grants two paid study afternoons; otherwise I'd keep current pay and use free library materials. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax post ends and the pension still cannot cover our bills, I'd take a posted funded meal-service role only with written bills-covering pay, signed start and hours fitting Owen's confirmed rota; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take only paid firm work still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current thin account, even with a long runway. Ten years is not ten years of savings yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children fund retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter may have a better job by 2036, but her wages are hers. Owen and I will look at the pension statement together and adjust only to an amount that is actually payable. I would rather keep earning than send her the mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid study time is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm denies paid study time, I will not take unpaid leave and call it preparation. I can read the free materials after work and keep the paid accounts rota while offered. If the hospital has no funded place later, I will search other posted meal-service roles rather than volunteer for a wage.

fieldNote: Her **age in 2036** is sixty-eight, but no pension entitlement or adequacy is presumed without an actual statement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the junior tax drafts that pay our mortgage could disappear quickly. Daily AI use helps me work now, but it does not guarantee the firm will keep paying me. A written wage bridge, funded learning, a paid trial shift and a real posted job would help. The mortgage needs paid hours, not a course badge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a restaurant worker gets help when a till export and the stock on a shelf disagree. I like following that trail and explaining it. Someone needs to pay for the visit and the correction, or it becomes free work.

headlineQuote: The mortgage needs paid hours, not a course badge.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Sara prepares restaurant accounts and tax-return drafts as a junior.
Her **accounting bachelor’s** accompanies below-average skill and continued senior review.
She uses **AI daily** to flag till differences but checks the source herself.
Owen’s **variable depot wage**, grown children, mortgage and sub-month savings keep money tight.
Few **nearby firms** and low pay make funded training and posted work important.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase the junior drafts that pay her mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written wage bridge**, funded learning, paid trial shifts and a real posted job.
